title: Search-Optimized Databases
summary: When LIKE queries stop working, use an inverted index and plan for freshness.
keyPoints: A leading-wildcard LIKE query scans text; an inverted index maps terms to the documents that contain them.
Analysis controls matching: tokenization, stemming, synonyms, and language rules must agree at index and query time.
Ranking is product logic, not only a text score; field boosts and recency change what users see first.
A search index is a derived copy, kept current through an outbox or change data capture with idempotent upserts.
Search freshness is a trade-off; state the lag and what users see while the index catches up.
Shards and replicas scale the index, while mapping changes usually require a parallel reindex and alias swap.

complexity.note: Writes also update segment structures and replicas.
Phrase and fuzzy queries read more postings.

complexity.time: O(m log k) for m matches
depends on edit distance and term count

complexity.note: Backfill, replay changes, then switch the alias.

commonMistakes: Treating the search index as the source of truth instead of a derived copy.
Using LIKE with a leading wildcard on a large text column and expecting an index to help.
Mismatching the index-time and query-time analyzers, then wondering why relevant documents are missing.
Ignoring index lag and showing users a search result that omits the item they created seconds ago.
interviewNotes: Explain why a normal B-tree index cannot serve free-text search, then introduce the inverted index.
Name the freshness path: outbox or CDC, idempotent upserts, version checks, and reconciliation.
Describe ranking signals and say which ones are product policy rather than text relevance.
State the stale window and the fallback when the search cluster is unavailable or behind.
Cover sharding, replicas, deep pagination, and the cost of a reindex.

checkYourself.question: Why does an inverted index make text search faster than a table scan?
checkYourself.answer: It maps each term directly to the documents that contain it, so a query reads only the relevant postings lists instead of every row.

checkYourself.question: Why must index-time and query-time analyzers match?
checkYourself.answer: The query must produce the same terms that were stored. If one side stems or normalizes differently, the terms will not match.

checkYourself.question: How do you keep a search index fresh without dual-writing synchronously?
checkYourself.answer: Commit the record and an outbox event in one database transaction, publish the event asynchronously, and have an idempotent indexer upsert by document id and version.
